title: Neither green nor blue
hookLine: from his tutor: not to take sides at the chariot races, to work with his hands, and not to listen to slander (Meditations 1.5)
carry: watch the race, keep your head

cards: A racetrack packed all the way to the rails. Chariot teams, each in its own color. Fans who wore the colors, bet on them, argued over them.

Rome's races at the Circus Maximus drew huge crowds, and Marcus names two of the colors: the Greens and the Blues. A little boy in Rome would have heard which side everyone was on. His tutor taught him something else.

teach.b: First, the tutor. Section five begins, From my governor. Marcus never names him: the man who looked after and taught him as a boy, whose lessons made the list.

teach.h: NO GREEN, NO BLUE, NO GLADIATOR TEAM.
teach.b: In Long's translation, Marcus learned from him "to be neither of the green nor of the blue party at the games in the Circus," nor a fan of one kind of gladiator over another.
The fan clubs were loud and loyal, and the tutor told a boy who would one day sit in the emperor's box: don't belong to a color. Third, the rest of the list.

teach.h: HARD WORK, LITTLE WANTS, NO SLANDER.
teach.b: The same tutor taught him to put up with hard work, to want little, to work with his own hands, not to meddle in other people's business, and not to be quick to listen to slander.
The thread: every item is about not being pulled. Not by a crowd's color, or comfort, or other people's affairs, or gossip about someone. Fourth, why it lasts.
Marcus didn't have to avoid the games; as emperor, he'd be expected to show up. The lesson wasn't, never enjoy a race.

teach.h: DON'T HAND YOUR MIND TO A TEAM.
teach.b: It was, don't hand your mind to a team. That lands differently now, in a world of team colors, party colors and online feuds where the first question is often which side are you on.
The tutor's answer was simple, and a little brave: neither.

how: Some readers of the Meditations take this line as a reason to step back from fan rivalries, office factions and online feuds, and to work with their hands and avoid gossip.

o: a chariot driver who raced at the Circus Maximus
a Roman fact, written down and sworn as true
a team or party, like Rome's Greens and Blues

games.q: neither green nor blue — tap the pairs.
p: not to be quick to listen

s: Marcus names the tutor who taught him this
he only says 'from my governor'; the name is lost.
the tutor also taught him to work with his own hands
along with enduring hard work and wanting little.
as emperor, Marcus refused ever to attend the games
nothing says he stayed away; the lesson was not to hand his mind to a team.

games.q: you're the boy Marcus at the Circus. everyone around you is wearing green or blue and shouting. what do you do?
o: watch the race, and take neither side.
games.why: his tutor taught him to be neither of the green nor of the blue party. he wrote it down decades later, as emperor.

practice: Bring to mind one rivalry you've joined by habit: a fan feud, an office camp, an argument between two sides online. Picture taking off the color, folding it, and setting it down; you can still watch the race.
Notice what changes in your chest, and breathe there.

wordCard.voice: Factio. Latin for a party or team, like the Greens and Blues: Marcus's boyhood tutor taught him not to join the chariot-racing factions, or the gossip, or any crowd that pulls the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a party or team. The Greens and Blues were factiones, the racing companies and their fans.

carryVoice: Your line: watch the race, keep your head. You can enjoy the game without handing your mind to a team. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: to be neither of the green nor of the blue party at the games in the Circus
